title: The Cognitive Bias That Made a Village Starve Because of a Full Moon
hook: Every month, the entire village refused to eat for three days—not due to ritual, but because a single lunar phase convinced them food was poison.
why_this_can_go_viral: A real cognitive bias causing deadly behavior is shocking and shareable—people love 'stupid human tricks' that end tragically.

why_this_can_go_viral: The violation of the sacred mother-child bond and the invisible trigger make this deeply unsettling and highly shareable.

hook: A single recording of a dog barking, played at a specific frequency at 3 AM each night, drove an entire neighborhood to flee within two weeks.

title: The Cognitive Bias That Made a Teacher Fail Every Student Named Michael
hook: A tenured professor gave lower grades to every 'Michael' for 15 years—not consciously, but because her first love who broke her heart was named Michael.
why_this_can_go_viral: Personal relatability (everyone has a name) plus systemic injustice creates high engagement and comment potential.

hook: The government tracked which ice cream flavors sold in each district—when 'chocolate' dropped, they sent in troops before a single protest began.
why_this_can_go_viral: The absurdity of using dessert preferences for oppression makes it incredibly viral—'they're watching what you eat' is a great hook.

title: The Manipulation Tactic That Used a Broken Glass to Frame a CEO for Murder

why_this_can_go_viral: The long-term nature of the manipulation ('months later') shocks viewers and makes them wonder what setups they might be in.

title: The Real Mind Control Experiment That Used a Flashlight to Induce Amnesia
hook: Subjects stared at a pulsing light for 20 minutes. When it stopped, they couldn't remember their own name, their family, or the experiment—ever again.
why_this_can_go_viral: The idea that a simple light can wipe memory feels like sci-fi but is real—viewers will demand proof and share out of disbelief.

why_this_can_go_viral: Betrayal, war, and invisible mind control combine for maximum dark fascination—military and psychology audiences collide.
